content: 1. Fortified milk and its associated outcomes in children aged 12–23 months were studied by Ana C. Fernández-Gaxiola, Luz María De-Regil, and Sandra Gallegos-Lecona. The research was conducted at the National Institute of Public Health in Mexico City, Mexico, and LMD Inc. in Toronto, Canada, with one author currently affiliated with the WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis on the optimal timing for introducing complementary feeding was conducted by Jai K. Das, Zahra A. Padhani, Faareha A. Siddiqui, Rehana A. Salam, Zohra S. Lassi, Durray Shahwar A. A. Abbasi, and Emily C. The study involved institutions such as Aga Khan University in Karachi, Pakistan; the Melanoma Institute Australia at the University of Sydney; the Robinson Research Institute at the University of Adelaide; the Centre for Global Child Health at The Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, Canada; and Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health in the United States. 3. The WHO conducted a systematic review on complementary feeding of animal-source foods, led by Zohra S. Lassi, Komal Abdul Rahim, Christina Oh, Kimberly Charbonneau, Aatekah Owais, Emily Keats, and Zulfiqar A. Bhutta. The research was carried out at the Robinson Research Institute in Adelaide, Australia; Aga Khan University in Karachi, Pakistan; and the Centre for Global Child Health in Toronto, Canada. 4. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the consumption of fruits, vegetables, pulses, nuts, and seeds among children aged 6–23 months and their association with dietary and health outcomes. This study was conducted by Leila Harrison, Christina Oh, Kimberly D. Charbonneau, Aatekah Owais, Emily C. Keats, and Zulfiqar A. Bhutta at the Centre for Global Child Health in Toronto, Canada. 5. The impact of greater consumption of unhealthy foods and beverages on malnutrition and diet-related non-communicable diseases in children under 10 years was systematically reviewed by Emily K. Rousham, Sophie Goudet, Oonagh Markey, Ben Boxer, Paula Griffiths, Emily Petherick, and Rebecca Pradeilles. The research was conducted at Loughborough University in the United Kingdom, the University of Sheffield in the United Kingdom, and Addis Ababa University in Ethiopia. 6. A systematic review on the health outcomes associated with fortified complementary foods was conducted by Ildikó Csölle, Regina Felső, Éva Szabó, Maria-Inti Metzendorf, Lukas Schwingshackl, Tamás Ferenci, and Szimonetta Lohner. The study involved institutions such as the University of Pécs in Hungary, Heinrich-Heine-University Düsseldorf in Germany, the University of Freiburg in Germany, and Óbuda University in Hungary. 7. A systematic review and meta-analysis on the safety and effectiveness of responsive feeding for infants and young children was conducted by Natalia Elorriaga, Ariel Bardach, María Victoria Lopez, Milagros García Diaz, Federico Rodriguez Cairoli, Marión Figarella de Aguirre, Gabriela Olivera y Luna, Daniel Comandé, Vilma Irazola, and Agustín Ciapponi. The research was carried out at the Institute for Clinical Effectiveness and Health Policy (IECS) and the Center for Research in Epidemiology and Public Health (CIESP) in Buenos Aires, Argentina. 8. Qualitative systematic reviews were conducted to assess the impact of complementary feeding recommendations on preferences, equity, rights, resource implications, acceptability, and feasibility. This research was led by Reginald Adjetey Annan, Nana Ama Frimpomaa Agyapong, Linda Nana Esi Aduku, Odeafo Asamoah Boakye, and Michael Wiafe Akenteng at the College of Science, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi, Ghana. 9. The WHO guideline for complementary feeding of infants and young children aged 6–23 months includes a summary of core food groups and subgroups used in modeling studies. These include dairy products, protein foods, legumes, nuts, seeds, meats, fish, and added fats and oils. 10. The guideline also evaluates the consumption of animal milk versus milk formula and follow-up formula in children aged 6–23 months. The benefits, harms, certainty, and balance of these feeding practices are assessed, with considerations for values, preferences, resources, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. 11. The impact of greater consumption of unhealthy foods and beverages, such as those high in sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats, as well as sugar-sweetened beverages, was reviewed. The findings suggest that reducing consumption of these items likely favors better health outcomes, though uncertainties remain regarding harms and cost-effectiveness. 12. Interventions incorporating responsive feeding elements were found to have moderate benefits and minimal harms. These interventions are likely to be cost-effective and feasible, with varying levels of acceptability and resource implications.
